newsitem.title: UGANDA: Economic gloom hangs over Africa's free market leader.
newsitem.headline: Economic gloom hangs over Africa's free market leader.

text.p: Uganda faces a turbulent economic year and recession after a boom period when it was top of the class in Africa, financial and government leaders commented on Friday in reactions to the budget.
As gloom set in after Thursday's budget, they blamed the setback on the combined effects of drought, corruption, regional rebellions and fiscal indiscipline.

Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni told parliament on Thursday that he would appeal for international food aid following severe food shortages in some districts and that corruption had seriously undermined revenue collection.
Presenting the 1997/98 budget, Finance Minister Jehoash Mayanja-Nkangi said civil war in northern and southwestern Uganda impeded revenue collection and undermined agricultural production.
Financial indiscipline meant government cash was not used for budgeted projects, he said.
An executive with leading manufacturers Mukwano Industries said Uganda was facing severe recession and efforts to promote industry were undermined by a shortage of money in the economy.
A leading banker added that the business outlook for the year was very bleak and that Ugandans had to reluctantly admit that years of dramatic economic growth were finally over.
"We are already in recession. For manufacturers, there is no money on the buy side because goods are pretty expensive and the ordinary people have no money," said the Mukwano executive.
A central bank official saw major changes as the freeing of capital accounts and further trader reforms, which would encourage foreign investment to try to bolster the economy.
There was general gloom in government, where spending was cut by as much as 30 percent. Salary rises and recruitment of public servants were put on hold until conditions improved.
Mayanja-Nkangi saved money for universal primary education, a campaign pledge by the president to offer free education in primary school for four children per Ugandan family.

But Uganda's Association of Manufacturers saw progress with Mayanja-Nkangi's pledge to repair roads, water, power and telecommunications and were pleased with cash set aside funds for industrial estates to help create jobs for the poor state.

Uganda's economy grew by only 5.0 percent in 1996/97 from 8.2 percent in 1995/96. It is forecast to grow at 7.0 percent in 1997/98. Inflation rose to 11.8 percent in 1996/97 from a single digit but will ease to 7.5 percent in 1997/98, the minister said.
Museveni said he would propose laws that forced peasants to plant food to avoid shortages in the future. He would also deploy troops to help old couples plant their coffee.
Mayanja-Nkangi launched major reforms in the revenue collection and customs areas, as well as in trade laws to cut corruption.

He removed tax holidays for foreign investors and ended all tax exemptions on government procurements to check abuse. He said as many as 100,000 Ugandan companies did not pay tax mainly because of poor supervision but that would now end.
Nkangi made no provisions for institutional support for the Uganda Securities Exchange (bourse) as requested by brokers.
Brokers said with such tight spending, they had expected little and planned to start trading on the bourse in a month.

There were no budget provisions regarding coffee. William Naggaga of the Uganda Coffee Development Authority told Reuters despite the threat by coffee wilt disease, Uganda was still on course to export up to 4.0 million bags in 1996/97. He gave no forecasts for 1997/98.
($1=1070 Ugandan shillings)
